issues.title: Invalid infinite Taylor expansion
issues.failure_explanation: For a fixed finite odd n, the proof writes the sampled expression as an exactly equal infinite Taylor series. For example, the smooth flat function f(a)=0 and f(x)=exp(-1/(x-a)^2) for x different from a has every derivative at a equal to zero but has nonzero samples at a+xi_k h, so the asserted series side vanishes while the sampled expression does not. Only derivatives through n are needed, and finite Taylor expansion supplies them with an o(h^{n+1}) remainder.
issues.overall_effect: The coefficient-matching proof rests on a false intermediate identity. The Newton–Cotes identification itself can be recovered unchanged by using finite Taylor's theorem.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the asserted exact infinite Taylor series in the Newton–Cotes coefficient-matching step by Taylor's formula truncated at j=n with an o(h^{n+1}) remainder. Matching the coefficients for j=2,...,n then gives the same linear system; for the relevant polynomials the remainder vanishes, so the Newton–Cotes identification is unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The infinite equality is genuinely false for smooth nonanalytic functions, so the proof needs a remainder argument rather than a transcription-only correction. Finite Taylor's theorem provides a short, routine, local repair that preserves the result and its guarantees without a new lemma or proof architecture.

issues.title: Malformed second sample in outlook formula
issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims an o(h^4) two-point quadrature and identifies f_0 and f_1 as its inputs. The paper's general definition makes every such input a value of f at a node, but the old clause sets f_1 equal to a+(1-xi)h itself. Thus it supplies an abscissa rather than the second sample. Concretely, for f identically 1 and a=2, the printed inputs satisfy f_0=1 and f_1 tending to 2, so q tends to 1/log(2)-log(2)/12 rather than 1 and the quadrature error is O(h), not o(h^4).
issues.overall_effect: The prospective rule is not a two-sample quadrature as printed and can fail even on a constant integrand. No formal result depends on this outlook claim.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the printed definition f_1=(a+(1-ξ)h) by f_1=f(a+(1-ξ)h), restoring the second input as the function value at the reflected node.
issues.why_classification: The general definition of quadrature inputs, the definition of f_0, and the description as a two-point rule uniquely force the omitted function application. This is a transcriptional wrong-object error requiring no mathematical inference or dependent repair.

issues.title: Wrong sign in the fourth-order two-point formula
issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims an o(h^4) two-point rule. Reading f_1 as the independently forced sample f(a+(1-xi)h), take f(x)=e^x and xi=(3-sqrt(3))/6. Direct expansion of the printed minus-sign rule gives hq-I[f]=-e^{a+h/2}h^3/18+O(h^5), so its error is O(h^3), not o(h^4). Changing the minus sign to plus cancels that term and leaves an O(h^5) error.
issues.overall_effect: The prospective rule has only O(h^3) local error on an exponential instead of the advertised o(h^4) error. No formal result depends on the outlook formula.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the sign of the second term from minus to plus: q(f_0,f_1)=(f_0-f_1)/log(f_0/f_1)+(f_0-f_1)log(f_0/f_1)/12. With ξ=(3-√3)/6, a midpoint expansion then gives q=f(a+h/2)+h^2 f''(a+h/2)/24+O(h^4), so the local quadrature error is O(h^5), hence o(h^4).
issues.why_classification: The advertised fourth-order accuracy, the fixed symmetric nodes, and the coefficient magnitude uniquely force the positive sign: the printed negative sign leaves an h^3 error term. A one-symbol transcription correction restores the intended guarantee, and no proof or downstream result requires further repair.
